text: A causal language model reads a sequence from left to right. At each position, it predicts the token that follows the tokens it has already seen.
A tokenizer converts text into integer token identifiers. The same tokenizer must be used during training, evaluation, and generation.
Continued pretraining adapts an existing base model to a new collection of text. The objective remains next-token prediction.
A training split is used to update model parameters. A validation split is kept separate and is used to estimate performance on unseen documents.
Data leakage occurs when the same document appears in both training and validation data. Deduplication should happen before the dataset is split.
A batch contains several token sequences processed together. Larger batches can produce stable gradients, but they also require more memory.
Gradient accumulation simulates a larger batch. The optimizer updates the model only after gradients from several smaller batches have been accumulated.
The learning rate controls the size of each optimization update. A rate that is too large can damage pretrained knowledge, while a very small rate can make adaptation slow.
A checkpoint stores model weights, optimizer state, scheduler state, and training progress. It allows an interrupted experiment to resume.
Perplexity is derived from the average language-model loss. Lower perplexity indicates that the model assigns higher probability to the held-out text.
A reproducible experiment records the model revision, dataset version, random seed, package versions, hardware, and training configuration.
Padding makes variable-length examples fit into one batch. Padding positions use a label of minus one hundred so they do not contribute to the loss.
An end-of-sequence token marks a document boundary. It helps the model learn that one document has finished before another document begins.
Long documents are divided into chunks that fit the context window. Each chunk should contain at least two tokens for next-token prediction.
Evaluation data must not update model weights. It is used only to calculate metrics and compare experiments.
Python functions keep reusable operations in named blocks. Clear function names make a training pipeline easier to test and maintain.
A unit test supplies a known input and checks the resulting output. Useful tests focus on behavior that could fail during future changes.
Configuration files separate experiment settings from program logic. This makes it easier to repeat a run with different models or hyperparameters.
Before training a large model, run a tiny smoke test. A smoke test confirms that loading, tokenization, batching, loss calculation, evaluation, and saving all work together.
